_readme: WHAT EACH REPORT MODEL SERVES — read by the AI *and* by the Model Guide screen.
Asked for by Mike, 2026-08-21: 'ensure that each of the performance models have a
"key calculation output" page or section, so that the AI can read what the model
serves', and 'place it wherever you want, it's for AI - not the advisor or manager'.
To-do item 4.29. Plan item T22, feeding T23.
🔴 THIS FILE HAS TWO READERS: THE AI, AND THE MODEL GUIDE SCREEN AT /model-guide.
⚠ ONE FIELD IS THE EXCEPTION: `searchWords` is read ONLY by the screen's search box.
It is the everyday vocabulary an advisor types — "houses" for the property model — and it
never reaches the AI: formatReportModelsForPrompt reads named fields and does not read this
one. So it is not content that shapes advice, and needs no manager screen. Item 4.36.
The screen was built 2026-08-22 (68f5fae) and reads these records through
GET /api/report/model-guide. Change anything here and you change both.
⚠ THESE LINES SAID 'WHY THIS HAS NO SCREEN' UNTIL 2026-08-22 and were left standing
when the screen was built the next day; corrected in session 81 while closing item
4.34, together with the same stale claim in design/features/report-models.md §3a.
🔴 WHAT THE OLD NOTE GOT RIGHT AND WHAT IS STILL BINDING: NOBODY EDITS THIS CONTENT.
CLAUDE.md's ruling of 2026-08-16 is that every AI fix surfaces on a hub page. Mike
ruled this one out of the EDITING half himself, and the reason holds: a description
of what a calculation DOES is a fact about the maths, not authored advisory
judgement. Nobody at any tier gets to decide that Lease vs Buy answers a different
question than it answers. Content a tier may shape lives on a hub page and is
editable there; this is a label on a machine, so /model-guide only ever shows it.
⚠ If that ever stops being true — if a firm wants to say when ITS advisors should
reach for a model — that IS authored judgement and it needs an EDITABLE screen at
the mentor tier first, per the standing rule. Do not quietly widen this file to
hold it.
🔴 THE CONSTRAINT THAT DECIDES WHAT IS IN HERE: THE AI MUST NEVER RECOMMEND A MODEL
WITH NO PAGE. Eight models in utils/reportModelCatalogue.js are STATUS_SOON and have
no route. A summary for one of those would send an advisor to a screen that does not
exist — which is to-do item 4.15 happening again somewhere new. Only the models that
are STATUS_READY and carry a route appear here, keyed BY that route.
tests/unit/reportModelSummaries.test.js holds this file to the catalogue BOTH WAYS:
a summary for a model that is not ready fails, and a ready model with no summary
fails. So the day a SOON model goes live, the build says it needs an entry rather
than the model quietly staying invisible to the AI.
THE FIELDS, and why each is here:
answers      — the question the model exists to answer, in an advisor's words.
keyOutputs   — Mike's 'key calculation output': the ACTUAL headline figures the
screen puts in its hero band, so the AI names what the advisor will
see rather than something it invented. Kept in step with the
locale hero labels by hand; the guard test checks the count.
inputsNeeded — what the advisor must be able to supply. An advisor who cannot get
these numbers should not be sent to the model.
useWhen      — the client situations that genuinely point at it.
coach        — the reading the screen's Coach panel gives, with its figures written
as {named} gaps. 🔴 THE GAPS ARE FILLED BEFORE ANYBODY SEES THEM:
server/utils/reportModelFigures.js computes each model on its own
defaults, the Model Guide fills them in the firm's currency and the
AI's block fills them in the platform default. Until 2026-08-22 they
were written [like this] and filled by nothing, so the screen read
'takes [n] days' and the AI was handed the same — to-do item 4.34,
raised by Mike: 'it makes this section worthless'.
⚠ A GAP NEEDS A FIGURE. Adding {oneOfThese} without adding it to
reportModelFigures.js fails tests/unit/reportModelFigures.test.js.
⚠ WHERE A LINE DESCRIBES A PATTERN RATHER THAN ONE READING — the
three Cost of Capital verdicts, the per-property sentence — it is
written as prose with NO gap. A single number there would read as
the answer when the screen gives a different one every time.
limits       — 🔴 what it does NOT cover, said out loud. Taken from the security
document's own instruction, 'state honestly what each control does
NOT cover', and from each model file's own fidelity notes. A model
recommended without its limits is how an advisor promises a client
something the screen does not do.
instruction: These are the calculation models built into this app. Each one has a working page an advisor can open.
- Mention a model ONLY when it directly answers the client situation being discussed. It is a tool, not a recommendation to make for its own sake.
- When you do, give its exact page path from this list so the advisor can open it.
- NEVER name a model that is not in this list, and never invent a page path. If no model fits, say that plainly — the app has models for some questions and not others.
- Say what the model does not cover when that matters to the situation. The limits are listed for that purpose.
- A model marked "illustrative" uses teaching figures, not the client's accounts. Never describe its numbers as a picture of the client's business.

models.name: Working Capital Cycle
models.answers: How fast a fixed pot of cash recycles through stock and debtors, and what speeding that cycle up is worth in revenue and profit.
keyOutputs: Cycle factor — how many times a year the cash turns over
Annual revenue at that cycle speed
models.inputsNeeded: Initial investment and the share of it spent on plant and equipment; unit cost, mark-up and discount; days deliverable, days on hand, days receivable, days payable; monthly fixed costs.
models.useWhen: The client is profitable on paper but short of cash. Stock sits too long, customers pay slowly, or the owner asks where the money has gone. Also when they want to know what tightening terms is actually worth.
models.limits: Illustrative teaching figures — no client data goes into it. It shows the mechanics of a cycle, not this client's cycle.

heroFigures.label: Working-capital cycle
heroFigures.sub: days — cash tied up before you can trade again

heroFigures.label: Cycle factor
heroFigures.sub: × per year

heroFigures.label: Annual revenue
heroFigures.sub: from the capital employed

models.alsoOnScreen: Working capital, monthly cash sales, total units, contribution margin, cash reserve required, return on working capital, the annual cycle factor, and the difference against a saved scenario in both dollars and per cent.
coach: Watch the wheel: your {workingCapital} of working capital flows Cash → Stock → Sale → Debtors and back. Right now that takes {cycleDays} days, so it turns about {cycleFactor}× a month. Fixed costs sit outside the wheel — paid whether it turns or not.
If you cut it to {fasterDays} days, the wheel would turn {fasterFactor}× a month — about {fasterExtra} more revenue a year, at the same price.

models.name: Debtor Business Drag
models.answers: How much of a year's sales is not lost but merely DELAYED into next year because customers pay slowly — the drag — and how much two different collection profiles change it, month by month, including the deepest overdraft.
keyOutputs: Deepest cash low under the plan
Deepest cash low before the change
The effect of the decisions — the difference between the two
models.inputsNeeded: Twelve months of sales, and two collection profiles: the share collected in the same month, at one, two, three and four months, and the share written off.
models.useWhen: Overdraft pressure, slow payers, or the question of whether to chase debtors harder or simply arrange a bigger overdraft. It puts a number on the choice.
models.limits: Illustrative teaching figures — no client data goes into it. It models a collection profile, not this client's ledger.

heroFigures.label: Deepest cash low — your plan
heroFigures.sub: the worst month under the profile you set

heroFigures.label: Deepest cash low — Before
heroFigures.sub: the same month on the frozen comparison

heroFigures.label: Effect of your decisions
heroFigures.sub: better or worse at the worst month

models.alsoOnScreen: Both collection profiles in full (same month, one, two, three and four months, write-off), the drag difference between them, monthly stock paid, months in overdraft, and the year-end balance.
coach: Cash arrives late — customers pay across the months after the sale — but suppliers, wages and GST don't wait. Your bank dips to {deepestLow} in {deepestLowMonth}, into overdraft, and you're in the red {monthsInOverdraft} months.
Collect earlier or pay suppliers slower and the blue line lifts; let collection drift later and you're forced to stretch suppliers, choking stock — the working capital cycle running backwards.

models.name: EBITDA & Discounted Cash Flow
models.answers: What the business is worth — normalised earnings before interest, tax and depreciation, and what its future cash is worth in today's money.
keyOutputs: Normalised EBITDA for the latest year
models.inputsNeeded: Several years of profit and loss, the normalisation add-backs, and the discount rate for each projected year. There is an optional listed-company block comparing an assessed share price against the market price.
models.useWhen: A sale, a purchase, a succession plan, a shareholder buy-out, or simply the owner asking what the business is worth.
models.limits: Two parts of the source workbook do NOT port and are not in this model: the interest calculations, and the margin-of-error and capitalised-earnings workings. Each projected year is discounted once at that year's rate rather than compounded — the source's own convention. It takes the client's real accounts, so it is never illustrative.

heroFigures.label: Enterprise Value
heroFigures.sub: 5-yr discounted cash flow + terminal

heroFigures.label: Normalised EBITDA (latest year)
heroFigures.sub: after owner-pay normalisation

heroFigures.label: Discounted 5-yr cash flow
heroFigures.sub: across the projected years

heroFigures.label: Terminal value
heroFigures.sub: final year × exit multiple

models.alsoOnScreen: Actual growth year by year and the average of it, the projected EBITDA series, and the sum of the discounted years. An optional listed-company block compares an assessed share price against the market price.
coach: {years} years of accounts show normalised earnings moving from {from} to {to} — average actual growth {avgGrowth}. On your projected growth and discount rates, the business supports an enterprise value of {enterpriseValue}.
Note the {dipYear} dip ({dipGrowth}) — growth is not a straight line, and a buyer will ask about that year.
The valuation is sensitive to the exit multiple: at {exitMultiple} the terminal value is {terminalShare} of the total — test it either side before quoting a range.

Where the numbers do not support a price it says so instead: “On these figures the valuation is not positive — the projected cash flows do not support a price. That is the honest read: the conversation is about restoring earnings before it can be about value.”

models.name: Margin · Mark-up · Break-even
models.answers: The pricing trio every quote depends on: the difference between margin and mark-up, the sales needed to break even, and what a price change does to the volume required to hold the same profit. The whole model rests on one rule — required sales = (overheads + the owner's drawings) ÷ margin.
models.inputsNeeded: Selling price and unit cost; overheads; the owner's target drawings; and the price change to test.
models.useWhen: Any pricing conversation. Discounting, quoting, a proposed price rise, or the classic question — if I drop the price ten per cent, how much more do I have to sell?
models.limits: Illustrative teaching figures — no client data goes into it. It is a calculator for the arithmetic of pricing, not a costing system.

heroFigures.label: Margin
heroFigures.sub: of the sale price

heroFigures.label: Mark-up
heroFigures.sub: of the cost price

heroFigures.label: Cost of sales
heroFigures.sub: of each sale dollar

heroFigures.label: Break-even · monthly
heroFigures.sub: units to cover it

coach: Same deal, two numbers: your margin is {margin} (of the sale) but your mark-up is {markup} (of the cost) — don't confuse them when you quote.

To cover {overheads} overheads and take {drawings} in drawings, you must sell {requiredSales} a month. Cut the price and that work climbs fast; raise it and it drops away. Price and drawings decide how hard the business has to run.

models.name: 8 Levers Model
models.answers: Which of the eight levers moves profit most, and which to pull first. The chain runs market size, foot traffic, prospects, customers, average spend, average frequency, revenue, margin, activity costs, fixed costs, profit — and the teaching point is that small nudges compound.
models.inputsNeeded: Either a trading position (a five-line product and labour mix, activity costs, fixed costs) or a set of funnel assumptions. It runs both ways.
models.useWhen: Growth planning, and the question of where to start. It is strongest when an owner believes only one lever matters — usually more sales — and needs to see the others.
models.limits: 🔴 EVERY figure in it is illustrative teaching data, including the 880,000 trading income. It is never a description of a real business. One known oddity is reproduced from the source rather than repaired: on the Scenarios sheet the current column is anchored to trading revenue while options B and C are built forward from the funnel, so the sheet's own profit increase reads as a large negative. That is the workbook's, not a fault in the client's numbers, and it should not be explained to a client as a finding.
models.alsoOnScreen: The full lever chain with each step's contribution, options B and C side by side against the current position, the profit increase in dollars and per cent, and a labour panel comparing charge-out rate against true cost per hour.
coach: On the chain: “Every customer is won through this chain. Each step multiplies the last — which is why a small gain early compounds all the way to revenue.”
On the comparison: “Look at Option C: it earns LESS revenue than Option B, yet makes MORE profit — because the margin lever outweighs the volume lever. That is the whole lesson.”

On labour: “What the business charges per hour against what it actually pays per hour — once leave, sick days and non-chargeable time are taken out. The labour lines look far more profitable on paper than they are in practice.”

models.name: Cost of Capital (WACC)
models.answers: What the money funding this business actually costs, blending what the owners expect on their equity with what the bank charges on debt. The result is the hurdle an investment has to clear to be worth doing.
models.inputsNeeded: Equity and debt amounts and rates, the tax rate, and a beta. There is a helper that derives a growth rate and two candidate betas from a pasted series of index values and shareholders' equity.
models.useWhen: Is this investment worth doing? Setting a hurdle rate, weighing a capital-structure change, or testing whether a project clears the cost of the money behind it.
models.limits: The beta helper OFFERS a beta; the person using the model decides whether to take it. That relationship is deliberate and comes from the source workbook. It takes the client's real numbers, so it is never illustrative and the privacy boundary applies.

heroFigures.label: Weighted average cost of capital
heroFigures.sub: the hurdle an investment must clear

heroFigures.label: Cost of equity
heroFigures.sub: what the owners' money expects to earn

heroFigures.label: Cost of debt (after tax)
heroFigures.sub: the borrowing rate, less the tax saved

heroFigures.label: Funded by equity
heroFigures.sub: and the balance funded by debt

models.alsoOnScreen: A beta helper deriving a growth rate, two candidate betas, average, standard deviation and volatility from a pasted index series — and a Test an investment panel that judges a specific investment against the hurdle.
coach: Test an investment takes what the investment costs and what it should earn each year, and returns one of three verdicts: that it clears your cost of capital by a stated number of percentage points, that it exactly meets it, or that it falls short by a stated number of percentage points.
It states its own strictness: “The bar is your cost of capital exactly as calculated above, with no safety margin added.”
It also warns when it cannot be trusted — too few periods to measure a spread, a beta outside the usual 0.3 to 2.5 range, or an index that does not move.

models.name: Lease vs Buy
models.answers: Whether leasing or buying an asset — a vehicle in the source model — costs less over its whole life, and which of the two to recommend.
models.inputsNeeded: Asset price; loan amount, rate, term and amortisation method; depreciation method and rate; running costs; the lease term, payments and lease-end costs; and the tax rate.
models.useWhen: Funding a vehicle or a piece of equipment, and the client is weighing a lease against a loan.
models.limits: The workbook's separate FBT-versus-reimbursement sheet is NOT part of the verdict and is not built — if the question is really about fringe benefit tax, this model does not answer it. It takes the client's real numbers, so it is never illustrative.

heroFigures.label: Total cost to buy
heroFigures.sub: over the whole term, after resale

heroFigures.label: Total cost to lease
heroFigures.sub: over the whole term, after residual

heroFigures.label: You save
heroFigures.sub: by choosing the cheaper option

coach: The model does not leave the choice open. It returns a one-word verdict — “Lease!” or “Buy!” — with the line: “That’s the cheaper option — {saving} less over the term.”

models.name: The Loan Estimator
models.answers: What lenders would lend against the security the client owns, whether the household can service it, and what the repayments would be.
keyOutputs: Available security — the unused lending headroom
models.inputsNeeded: Each security item the client owns — its class, market value, current debt, growth prospects and any value adjustment — plus household income and existing commitments.
models.useWhen: Borrowing capacity, refinancing, or a client asking whether the bank will lend for a purchase and whether they can afford it.
models.limits: The stress-tested payment is the BANK's worst-case figure — the full lending limit at the assessment rate over the maximum term — not the client's actual loan terms, and it should never be described as their repayment. The lending rules themselves come from a configuration file rather than from any one bank. It takes the client's real numbers, so it is never illustrative.

heroFigures.label: Maximum business loan
heroFigures.sub: against the business, on its EBIT — an indication only

heroFigures.label: Monthly surplus
heroFigures.sub: the number the affordability test is judged on

heroFigures.label: Available security
heroFigures.sub: across all assets, after existing debt

heroFigures.label: Monthly repayment
heroFigures.sub: on the proposed loan from the quick calculator

heroFigures.label: Estimated maximum borrowing
heroFigures.sub: with everything else as entered — an indication only

models.alsoOnScreen: Current equity, the stressed deposit required and the stress payment gap, debt-to-value / equity-to-value / loan-limit-to-value ratios, a household serviceability breakdown with the tax bands used, and a ten-year overdraft interest and closing-balance table.
coach: It reaches a verdict on affordability — “Meets the affordability test” or “Falls short of the affordability test” — immediately qualified: “An indication of affordability only — not a lending decision.”

The serviceability panel shows its working: total net monthly income, minimum monthly loan payments, and the monthly expenses used — “the greater of actual expenses and the bank's minimum allowances”.

models.name: Multiple Property Assessment
models.answers: Whether a rental property is worth buying, and whether a household's portfolio of up to five works — ten years of cash flow, tax with ring-fenced losses carried forward, both loans amortised, and the equity position.
models.inputsNeeded: Per property: purchase price, rent, operating costs and loan structure. For the portfolio: the family home and the loan apportionment across the properties.
models.useWhen: A client is buying a rental, or already owns several and wants to know whether the portfolio holds together over ten years rather than in the first month.
models.limits: Its tax treatment follows the firm's own Property Tax Rules settings — what may be depreciated, whether rental losses ring-fence, interest deductibility — which a group or firm manager sets. It is therefore the firm's stated position, not universal tax advice, and it is not a substitute for a tax opinion. It takes the client's real numbers, so it is never illustrative.

heroFigures.label: Weekly cash position
heroFigures.sub: year 1 — one property, or all of them

heroFigures.label: Total debt
heroFigures.sub: year 1

heroFigures.label: Net equity
heroFigures.sub: year 10

heroFigures.label: Return on investor funds
heroFigures.sub: year 10

models.alsoOnScreen: A ten-year investment summary: assumed property value, total debt position, net equity, cash deposit, annual cash top-up, capital introduced, cumulative investor funds, and the weekly cash profit or loss. Plus the loan apportionment across properties and the household's consolidated servicing.
coach: Per property it gives the weekly cost to the client and how long that lasts, the year it turns cash-positive, and the equity built over ten years against the money put in, as a rate of return. Where a property never turns, it says so.

On tax: either that no tax is payable across the ten years, or the year tax first becomes payable — and whether losses are ring-fenced against the property's own future income or offset against the client's other income.

Across the portfolio: whether the deposit stretches to every property, the combined loan to value against the ceiling, the ten-year cash demand on top of the deposit — closing on the question it is built to ask, which is not whether the portfolio grows but whether the family can carry the hardest year's weekly cost while it does.

models.name: Quick Position
models.answers: A fast read on where the business stands right now — how much cash it can actually reach, how long that lasts if sales stop, and what it must sell to break even.
models.inputsNeeded: Current cash, debtors, stock and creditors; monthly fixed costs; gross profit percentage; and any life-line capital the owner could call on.
models.useWhen: Distress, a sudden stop in trading, a lost major customer, or the owner asking how long they have. It is the model for the first conversation, not the detailed one.
models.limits: A service business with no stock removes the stock line from the model entirely rather than showing a misleading zero — set that, or the reading is wrong. Where a figure would divide by zero it returns nothing rather than a fabricated zero, so an unlimited runway shows as unlimited. The New Zealand COVID wage-subsidy block of the source workbook does not port. It takes the client's real numbers, so it is never illustrative.

heroFigures.label: Quick cash available
heroFigures.sub: realisable now, after immediate debts

heroFigures.label: Cover at zero sales
heroFigures.sub: months on the business's own resources

heroFigures.label: With life-line capital
heroFigures.sub: months, adding outside support

heroFigures.label: Break-even sales
heroFigures.sub: needed per month to stand still

coach: If sales stopped today, the business could cover its outgoings for {monthsZeroSales} months from its own quick cash — {monthsWithLifeline} months with the life-line capital. To stand still it needs {breakEvenSales} of sales a month at the current margin.
The discount trap: a {discount} discount means selling {salesIncrease} more just to keep the same gross profit.

Where the position is already negative it changes tone entirely: “Immediate debts exceed what the business can realise quickly. This is a now conversation: which creditors can wait, what can be turned to cash this week, and what outside support exists.”

models.name: Volatility Report
models.answers: How much a business swings from month to month, and whether those swings are its ordinary rhythm or something worth asking about. It draws the average through the monthly sales and puts bands at one, two and three standard deviations either side.
keyOutputs: Average monthly swing — the dial, 0 to 100
The normal range (one deviation either side)
How many months fall inside that range
models.inputsNeeded: Monthly sales, oldest first, over the most recent 12, 18 or 24 months. Nothing else — no costs, no balance sheet.
models.useWhen: The owner is reacting to every monthly figure, treating a good month as success and a bad one as failure. Also when someone asks whether a particular month was really a problem, or before setting a target off a single month.
models.limits: It says WHERE a month sits, never WHY. No statistic can separate a seasonal dip from a special cause from the business tampering with itself — that diagnosis is the adviser’s and the client’s. It uses the population standard deviation, describing the months in hand rather than estimating a wider population. The widest lower band can compute below zero; sales cannot be negative, so it stops at zero. It takes the client’s real numbers, so it is never illustrative.

heroFigures.label: Average monthly swing
heroFigures.sub: the dial: green under 50, red over 75

heroFigures.label: Average monthly sales
heroFigures.sub: the total over the months measured

heroFigures.label: Normal range
heroFigures.sub: one deviation either side

heroFigures.label: Months in range
heroFigures.sub: against the 68% the model expects

models.alsoOnScreen: The rev-counter dial, the monthly sales plotted against the bands, a table of the months that fall outside, and the highest and lowest month with their distance from the average.
coach: {n} of {of} months land inside the normal range — {pct}%, against the 68% the model predicts. Going up and down is normal. An owner who reacts to every month above or below the average is permanently passing or failing against a line that was never a target.
The report shows where a month sits. Whether it is seasonal, a one-off, or something the business did to itself is a judgement for the adviser and the client — not for the arithmetic.
